lines.text: VUGA NDAKUMVA INITIATIVE
Chapter 04
Understanding Consent,
Boundaries, and Bodily Autonomy
GBV Educational Content Library • Expanded Chapter 04 • Version 1.1 •
November 2026
PUBLICATION STATUS: Evidence-informed educational draft. Requires GBV/safeguarding, legal, clinical and
language review before public distribution.
Purpose and learning outcomes
Consent and bodily autonomy are essential to healthy relationships and freedom from coercion.
This chapter explains how people can recognize meaningful agreement, communicate limits,
respect others’ choices, and respond safely when power or fear makes agreement difficult. The
goal is education, not investigation, diagnosis or legal adjudication.
After studying this chapter, a reader should be able to explain informed and voluntary consent;
identify boundaries across physical, emotional, sexual and digital situations; recognize coercion
and power imbalances; discuss why silence or past agreement cannot replace present consent;
and identify safe options for seeking help.
01 | What consent means
Consent is a person’s voluntary, informed agreement to a specific action or interaction. The
person must be able to understand the choice and make it without threats, manipulation or other
coercion. Agreement should be communicated clearly, checked when uncertain, and revisited
when circumstances change. Consent is a process of respectful communication, not a signature,
ownership right, or permanent permission. [1, 2]
Consent matters in everyday life—touch, photographs, sharing personal information, medical
decisions and financial interactions. Sexual consent has special ethical and legal importance. The
fact that someone accepts one activity does not give permission for another.
Five practical characteristics of meaningful consent
• Freely given. A person can choose without fear, pressure, threats, punishment or exploitation.
• Informed. A person understands what is proposed and relevant conditions; deception about
material facts can undermine meaningful agreement.
• Specific. Permission applies to the particular action, not to every related action.

• Reversible. A person may stop or withdraw agreement at any time; previously agreed activity
must stop when consent ends.
• Clearly communicated. Seek an affirmative, understandable expression of willingness; do not
treat silence, freezing or non-resistance as permission.
These principles are useful educational guidelines; legal tests and definitions depend on the
applicable law and the circumstances. [1, 2, 3]
02 | Consent, choice and capacity
A meaningful choice requires more than a spoken “yes.” The setting must permit a real refusal. A
person who is asleep, unconscious or otherwise unable to understand or decide cannot provide
consent. Severe intoxication or incapacity can undermine the ability to consent; the precise legal
threshold requires case-specific assessment under applicable law. [1, 2]
Children have additional legal and safeguarding protections. Adult concepts of sexual agreement
must never be used to imply that a child can legally consent to sexual activity with an adult.
Age-of-consent and reporting obligations must be checked against current Rwanda law by a
qualified local reviewer before publication.
Silence, hesitation and survival reactions
Someone may become quiet, freeze, comply out of fear, or appear calm while feeling unsafe.
None of these responses proves agreement. A supportive person must not infer consent from a
lack of resistance; when uncertainty exists, pause and check, and stop if there is no clear freely
given agreement. A survivor should never be blamed for freezing or not physically resisting.
03 | Personal boundaries: understanding and expressing limits
A boundary is a limit that helps a person decide what they are comfortable sharing, doing, giving
or receiving. Boundaries may differ across people and situations; they can change over time. A
respectful boundary names what is acceptable and, when useful, what action the person will take
to protect their wellbeing. Respect for others is equally important.
• Physical: comfort with hugs, touching, personal space and privacy.
• Emotional: deciding whether to discuss a difficult experience or how much support to give.
• Sexual: deciding whether any sexual contact is wanted, and what kinds are not wanted.
• Digital: control over passwords, location sharing, photographs, messages and social media.
• Time and social: choosing when to rest, study, work or meet others, without unreasonable
control.
• Financial: deciding what money or possessions to share without threats or pressure.
Examples of respectful boundary statements
“I do not want to be hugged today.” “Please ask before posting my photo.” “I am not comfortable
sharing my password.” “I need to end this conversation for now.” “I can help tomorrow, but I
cannot do it tonight.”

People experiencing violence may be unable to express boundaries safely. It is not their
responsibility to confront someone who may retaliate. Safety takes priority over boundary-setting
exercises.
04 | Bodily autonomy and dignity
Bodily autonomy is the principle that people should be able to make decisions about their own
bodies free from violence and coercion, within applicable laws and protections. It includes the
right to personal safety, respect during healthcare, and freedom from unwanted contact. For
children and people needing decision-making support, autonomy must be understood alongside
safeguarding, accessible communication, and relevant legal requirements.
Respecting bodily autonomy means asking before touching where appropriate, explaining
proposed medical or intimate actions, and responding when a person expresses discomfort. A
person’s clothing, relationship status, disability, prior sexual experience, or dependence on others
does not cancel the need for consent.
05 | Coercion, manipulation and power imbalances
Coercion occurs when a person uses force, threats, intimidation, persistent pressure or
exploitation of vulnerability to influence another person’s choice. It may be physical, emotional,
economic, social or digital. A statement that sounds like agreement may not represent voluntary
consent if the alternative involves harm, punishment, lost housing or other serious consequences.
Recognizing tactics
• Threats: “If you refuse, I will hurt you or someone you care about.”
• Retaliation: threatening to withdraw income, accommodation or school support unless someone
complies.
• Guilt and persistence: repeated demands after a refusal or implying that love requires sexual
access.
• Misuse of authority: a teacher, employer, supervisor, religious leader or service provider linking
benefits to personal or sexual compliance.
• Isolation and monitoring: controlling friendships, travel, devices or communications to restrict
independent choices.
Power differences do not automatically make every relationship abusive, but they can make it
harder to refuse or raise concerns. Institutions should provide reporting channels that do not
require confronting the person with authority.
06 | Consent in dating, marriage and long-term relationships
Marriage, engagement, dating, cohabitation or previous sexual contact never creates permanent
consent. Each person retains the right to refuse sexual activity. A respectful partner asks rather
than assumes, accepts “no,” and does not punish refusal through anger, humiliation or financial
threats. [3, 4]

A relationship disagreement is not automatically GBV. However, repeated threats, forced sexual
contact, intimidation and control are significant warning signs. Supporters should examine safety
and patterns of control rather than telling a survivor to “communicate better” with an abusive
partner.
Checking in respectfully
Questions such as “Are you comfortable with this?”, “Do you want to continue?”, and “Would you
prefer to stop?” create space for choice. If a person hesitates or appears afraid, stop and avoid
pressure. Agreement to intimacy is not consent to contraception interference, recordings, or
dissemination of private material.
07 | Digital consent, privacy and technology
Digital consent applies when sharing photographs, recordings, messages, account access, contact
information, and location data. Permission to create a photo is not permission to publish or
forward it. Permission to use a shared device is not permission to read private messages or track
movements. Technology-facilitated GBV may include harassment, stalking, impersonation,
threats, and non-consensual sharing of intimate images. [5]
Practical safety options depend on context. For someone whose devices may be monitored,
changing a password, deleting messages or confronting a suspected abuser could increase
danger. Consider using a trusted device and obtaining confidential support. Do not assume a
“quick exit” button erases browsing history or makes a device safe.
Everyday examples
• A student agrees to join a class group; this does not permit classmates to publish personal
photographs without permission.
• A partner asks for continuous location access as “proof of loyalty.” A refusal should not trigger
threats or punishment.
• Someone forwards an intimate image originally shared in confidence. The original sharing does
not authorize further distribution.
08 | Culture, social expectations and unequal power
Families and communities differ in how they discuss personal space, sexuality and authority.
Cultural values such as mutual care and respect can strengthen prevention, while expectations
demanding unquestioning obedience or tolerating abuse can undermine choice. Education should
avoid stereotyping any community and should encourage discussion without forcing personal
disclosures.
In Rwanda, examples may involve university accommodation, workplace apprenticeships,
household decision-making, transportation, or online relationships. The examples below are
fictional and do not represent prevalence claims about any specific group.

09 | Scenario learning: four Rwanda-relevant cases
Scenario A — University study group
A student in Kigali is repeatedly pressured by a classmate to share private photos. The classmate
says they will spread rumors if the student refuses. This is not a freely chosen agreement; threats
and pressure are concerning. Safe options may include speaking to a trusted safeguarding officer
through a confidential channel and using a safe device for advice.
Scenario B — Supervisor and internship
An intern in Musanze is told that favorable evaluations depend on accepting unwanted personal
visits. The supervisor controls the evaluation, creating a serious power imbalance. The intern
should not be expected to confront the supervisor alone; an independent workplace reporting or
support route may be safer.
Scenario C — Marriage and financial control
One spouse threatens to withhold household necessities when the other refuses unwanted
intimacy. Relationship status does not remove the need for consent. Economic threats can
undermine free choice. Supporting the affected person means discussing safety and available
options without pressuring an immediate separation.
Scenario D — Shared smartphone
A young adult notices a partner may be monitoring a phone and demanding location sharing. A
friend suggests immediately changing all passwords on that phone. That action might be useful in
some settings, but it could trigger retaliation if the device is monitored. A safer first step may be
private advice from a trusted service using a device outside the partner’s control.
10 | How to respond when someone describes coercion
Listen with care and without interrogation. Ask what the person needs right now. Affirm that they
deserve safety and respect without making promises about outcomes. Explain confidentiality
limits, ask permission before making referrals wherever possible, and consider whether the
person can safely receive calls or messages. WHO’s LIVES approach offers a clinical first-line
support structure: Listen, Inquire about needs and concerns, Validate, Enhance safety, and
Support. [4, 6]
• Helpful: “Thank you for telling me. What would feel most helpful and safe right now?”
• Helpful: “You can choose what you share. I can explain support options.”
• Avoid: “Why didn’t you say no?”, “Why didn’t you leave?”, or “You must report immediately.”
• Avoid: pressuring someone into mediation or direct confrontation where violence or retaliation is
possible.

11 | Safety considerations and seeking support
If someone is in immediate danger or has a serious injury, urgent local emergency or medical
assistance is appropriate. After sexual assault, prompt medical attention can address injury and
time-sensitive preventive care; survivors can request information about medical options even
when unsure about reporting. Do not delay urgent care to complete exercises, preserve evidence
or finish reading this chapter.
In Rwanda, Isange One Stop Centres are an important integrated service model for survivors of
GBV. Local organizations should verify current access details, telephone numbers, hours, referral
criteria, and statutory reporting duties before publishing public instructions. This chapter
deliberately avoids unverified hotlines and jurisdiction-specific reporting promises.
For children, suspected abuse, or a person unable to make certain decisions, safeguarding duties
may differ from those for adults. Do not promise absolute secrecy. Explain relevant protections
and reporting requirements in age-appropriate language, and involve qualified safeguarding
professionals.
12 | Guided learning activities (optional and non-disclosing)
Activity 1 — Consent or pressure? (10 minutes)
Read each fictional sentence and decide whether it shows freely given agreement: (a) “Yes, I want
to participate,” after an open, pressure-free choice; (b) “Fine, I agree,” after threats to remove
financial support; (c) no reply while someone moves closer; (d) permission to share one
photograph privately. Suggested answers: (a) may indicate consent if informed, specific and the
person has capacity; (b) coercion undermines voluntary choice; (c) silence is not consent; (d)
permission does not extend to public posting.
Activity 2 — Everyday boundaries (10 minutes)
Write three harmless fictional situations involving shared space, photographs, and time. For each,
draft one respectful request and one respectful refusal. Example: “May I upload this photo?” / “No,
please keep it private.” No personal history is required.
Activity 3 — Power mapping (15 minutes)
Choose a fictional school or workplace situation. Identify who controls grades, pay, references,
accommodation, or reputation. Discuss what an independent reporting channel would look like
and how anonymity or confidentiality limits should be explained.
Activity 4 — Digital consent decision tree (10 minutes)
Imagine being asked to forward a friend’s personal message. Ask: Was permission given? For this
audience and purpose? Could sharing create harm? If permission is absent, do not share. If safety
is already threatened, seek appropriate support rather than negotiating with a threatening
person.

Activity 5 — Supportive response practice (15 minutes)
Using a purely fictional disclosure, practice a brief response that listens, validates, checks
immediate safety, and asks what assistance is wanted. Do not role-play graphic violence or
require participants to disclose personal experiences. Anyone may opt out.
13 | Knowledge assessment with explained answers
1. Does agreeing once mean consenting to every later activity?
Suggested answer: No. Consent is specific and can be withdrawn.
2. Is silence reliable evidence of consent?
Suggested answer: No. Silence or freezing may occur for many reasons; pause and seek clear
agreement.
3. Can a person refuse intimacy within marriage?
Suggested answer: Yes. Marriage is not permanent sexual consent.
4. What can make an apparent agreement coercive?
Suggested answer: Threats, retaliation, intimidation, exploitation of dependency, or pressure that
removes free choice.
5. Is consent to take a photo the same as consent to share it?
Suggested answer: No. Creation, storage and distribution are different acts requiring appropriate
permission.
6. Must a survivor confront a person who may retaliate?
Suggested answer: No. Safety and choice come first; independent support may be safer.
7. Why do authority relationships deserve extra care?
Suggested answer: Control over grades, work, money or services can make refusal difficult.
8. What should a supporter avoid after disclosure?
Suggested answer: Blame, interrogation, forced reporting, unsafe mediation and false
confidentiality promises.
9. What is a helpful first question?
Suggested answer: “What do you need right now, and is it safe for us to communicate?”
10. Is this handbook a legal or clinical diagnosis tool?
Suggested answer: No. It is educational and requires local specialist review before public use.

14 | Facilitator notes and accessibility
Use plain language, short sessions, and inclusive examples. Allow written, spoken or private
participation. Provide alternatives to pair work, and do not ask anyone to demonstrate consent
through physical touch. An educator should never invite public disclosures of abuse. Establish a
quiet opt-out option and identify an appropriate safeguarding contact before group sessions.
Translate carefully into Kinyarwanda and French. Concepts such as coercion, autonomy, consent
and abuse may not map perfectly word-for-word. Have a qualified local language reviewer and
GBV professional review both terminology and examples. For screen readers, keep headings
logical and avoid image-only explanations.
15 | Key terms
Consent: Voluntary, informed agreement to a specific act, communicated by someone able to
decide.
Bodily autonomy: The principle that a person should have agency over decisions involving their
body, subject to appropriate legal protections.
Boundary: A limit describing what a person is comfortable with or willing to do.
Coercion: Force, threats, pressure or exploitation that undermines meaningful free choice.
Power imbalance: A relationship where one person has substantially greater control over
resources, status or decisions.
Digital consent: Agreement about access, use or sharing of digital information, images and
communications.
Survivor-centred care: An approach prioritizing dignity, safety, confidentiality within its limits,
respect and informed choice.

17 | Publication approval checklist
• □ GBV specialist validates terminology, coercion examples and support principles.
• □ Rwanda-qualified legal reviewer checks current laws on consent, ages, confidentiality and
reporting.
• □ Clinical/safeguarding reviewer validates urgent care and referral language.
• □ Referral coordinator verifies actual local services and current contact details.
• □ Kinyarwanda and French versions are reviewed by qualified humans, not machine translation
alone.
• □ Accessibility and community user testing are completed without requiring survivors to disclose
experiences.
• □ Version number, approval owner and next review date are recorded.
Editorial caution: This document teaches principles and examples. It does not determine whether
a particular incident constitutes an offence, and it is not a substitute for emergency support,
clinical care or qualified legal advice.
